That line runs in the configuration phase, which evaluates every build script of every project on every single build — including one whose only task is `help`.

Gradle runs three phases in order:
1. **Initialization** — `settings.gradle.kts` is evaluated and Gradle decides which projects are part of the build.
2. **Configuration** — every project's build script is evaluated and the task graph is assembled. Nothing has run yet, but every top-level statement has.
3. **Execution** — only the requested tasks and their dependencies run their actions.

### What that means for a build script
- Anything at the top level of a build script — a `ProcessBuilder`, a file read, a network call, a `println` — is configuration work that every developer pays for on every invocation, whatever they asked Gradle to do.
- `tasks.create(...)` and `tasks.getByName(...)` configure the task eagerly, even when it never ends up in the graph. `tasks.register(...)` and `tasks.named(...)` defer that block until something actually needs the task. Use the lazy pair everywhere.
- Real work belongs in a `@TaskAction` or a `doLast { }`; the values that feed it belong in a `Provider`, which is computed only when someone reads it.

### The trap
Deferring is not the same as tracking. `providers.exec { }` and `providers.of(ValueSource) { }` are lazy *and* registered as configuration-cache inputs, so Gradle re-checks the value and otherwise reuses the cached configuration. A raw `ProcessBuilder` is neither: with the configuration cache on, its result is frozen into the cache entry and the build starts stamping yesterday's commit hash.

Mental model: configuration decides what to do, execution does it. A line that costs time without deciding anything is in the wrong phase.

`api` puts that dependency on the compile classpath of every consumer, so from now on any change to its public signatures recompiles all of them, transitively.

- **implementation** — used to compile this module and present at runtime for consumers, but absent from their compile classpath. Consumers recompile only when *your* module's ABI changes, never because your dependency changed its internals.
- **api** — everything `implementation` does, plus the dependency is visible to consumers at compile time. Correct only when the type appears in your public signatures: a return type, a parameter, a supertype, a public property, an annotation you re-expose.
- **compileOnly** — compile classpath only, not packaged and not on the runtime classpath. For annotations that vanish after compilation and for APIs the environment provides. Consumers see nothing; `compileOnlyApi` passes it on.
- **runtimeOnly** — packaged and on the runtime classpath, invisible while compiling. Drivers, logging backends, the implementation behind an interface you code against.

### Why the cascade happens
Gradle does compile avoidance by hashing the ABI of the compile classpath — public signatures, not method bodies. Change a body and consumers stay up to date; change a signature and everyone downstream recompiles. `api` pushes that blast radius one hop further out for every consumer, which is how a one-line edit in `:core` ends up rebuilding forty modules.

### The trap
"Cannot access class" usually means the leak is real — you are handing out someone else's type. The cheaper fix is often to stop exposing it: wrap it, or return your own type. Also note that `implementation` is not encapsulation at runtime; the classes are still packaged and still reachable by reflection, it only hides them from the compiler.

Rule of thumb: `api` for what is in your signatures, `implementation` for everything else.

A version catalog gives every module one typed name for a dependency you declare yourself; a BOM constrains the versions of artifacts you never named, including the ones that arrive transitively.

### The catalog
`gradle/libs.versions.toml` is picked up with no configuration and generates type-safe accessors:
- `[versions]` holds the numbers, `[libraries]` the coordinates with `version.ref`, `[bundles]` named groups, `[plugins]` plugin ids.
- `implementation(libs.androidx.core.ktx)` — dashes and underscores in a key become dots in the accessor.
- `implementation(libs.bundles.compose)` adds a whole group in one line.
- `alias(libs.plugins.android.application)` inside `plugins { }`; the plugin version is declared once, in the root project or in `pluginManagement`.
- A typo is a build-script compile error instead of a resolution failure two minutes later.

### What a catalog cannot do
It only touches the coordinates you write down. If Compose Foundation arrives transitively at a different version, Gradle resolves the conflict on its own and the catalog is never consulted. `implementation(platform(libs.compose.bom))` adds the family's published constraints, so every Compose artifact — declared or transitive — lands on the same release train, and you then declare those artifacts with no version at all.

### The trap
Accessors are generated for the build scripts of the main build, not for `buildSrc` or a `build-logic` plugin. In a convention plugin written as a class, read the catalog through `extensions.getByType<VersionCatalogsExtension>().named("libs")`; in a precompiled script plugin, `the<LibrariesForLibs>()`.

Rule of thumb: the catalog names the versions you choose, the BOM aligns the versions you inherit.

Twelve: the dimensions multiply with each other and the result multiplies by the build types, and every variant is a full set of compile, merge, lint and package tasks.

- **Build types** say *how* it is built — debuggable, minified, shrunk resources, which signing config, id and version suffixes. `debug` and `release` exist by default.
- **Product flavors** say *what* is built — a different application id, different code, different resources. Every flavor must name a `dimension`, and the order in `flavorDimensions` sets priority between them.
- A variant is one build type plus one flavor from each dimension: `free` x `play` x `debug` = `freePlayDebug`.

### Which source sets it compiles
All of `main`, `free`, `play`, `freePlay`, `debug`, `freeDebug`, `playDebug`, `freePlayDebug`. When they collide, priority runs highest first: the full variant, then flavor-combination-plus-build-type, then the build type, then the flavor combination, then the individual flavors in `flavorDimensions` order, then `main`.

Kotlin and Java sources are **additive** — the same class in `main` and in `free` is a duplicate-class error, not an override. Resources, assets and manifests **merge** — a drawable or a string in `src/free/res` replaces the one from `main`. So the way to swap an implementation per flavor is to define that class in *every* flavor of the dimension and not in `main` at all.

### The trap
Each dimension multiplies build time, CI time and Lint runs, and most combinations are never shipped. Turn them off with `androidComponents { beforeVariants(selector().withBuildType("release").withFlavor("store" to "huawei")) { it.enable = false } }` — the old `variantFilter` was removed in AGP 8. And a library module that does not declare a dimension the app has needs `missingDimensionStrategy`.

Three separate mechanisms: generated constants for values the code reads, an id suffix and manifest placeholders for identity, and a per-variant source set for files.

### Values the code reads
- `buildConfigField("String", "API_URL", "\"https://staging.api.example.com\"")` generates a field into `BuildConfig`. Since AGP 8.0 it needs `buildFeatures { buildConfig = true }` — the flag is off by default now.
- `resValue("string", "build_label", "STAGING")` generates a resource instead, which is what a manifest or an XML layout can reference. The name must not also exist in `src/main/res`, or you get a duplicate-resource error.
- `manifestPlaceholders["deepLinkHost"] = ...` fills `${deepLinkHost}` in `AndroidManifest.xml` — the usual home for API keys, deep-link hosts and provider authorities.

### Identity
`applicationIdSuffix = ".staging"` gives the build a different package name so it installs beside production, and `versionNameSuffix` labels it. Keep the two ids straight: `namespace` is compile-time — where `R` and `BuildConfig` are generated — and never varies per variant; `applicationId` is the identity on the device and does.

### Files
Drop the icon in `src/staging/res/mipmap-*/`, a second Firebase config in `src/staging/google-services.json`, a different `Analytics.kt` in `src/staging/kotlin/`. The variant's source set overlays `main`, so nothing branches anywhere in the code.

The trap is everything keyed to the application id: OAuth clients, the Firebase app, deep-link `assetlinks.json` and any hardcoded `com.example.app` string now have to exist twice. And `initWith(getByName("release"))` copies `isMinifyEnabled` along with the rest — which is what you want from a staging build, as long as you also upload its mapping file.

Rule of thumb: if the value differs, generate it; if the file differs, overlay it; if the identity differs, suffix it.

kapt runs Java annotation processors, and they cannot read Kotlin, so before any processing it converts every Kotlin file in the module into a Java stub and compiles those; KSP reads Kotlin symbols directly through its own resolver and skips the step entirely.

### What each one costs
- kapt: stub generation, then javac processing rounds, then Kotlin compilation. Stubs are produced for the whole module, so the cost scales with module size, not with how many classes are annotated.
- KSP: a single pass over Kotlin symbols with an incremental Gradle task. Google measures roughly a 2x improvement on processor-heavy modules; how much you actually get depends on how much of that module's time was stubbing.
- kapt is in maintenance mode. It works with K2 — the default since Kotlin 2.1.20 — but gets no new features, and JetBrains points new work at KSP.

### What migrating actually breaks
- Every processor in the module needs a KSP implementation. Room, Moshi, Dagger/Hilt and Glide have one; Data Binding does not, so a module using it stays on kapt.
- A processor is not something you can adapt yourself: KSP's `SymbolProcessor` is a different API from `javax.annotation.processing.Processor`, so if the library has not shipped one, you wait or you fork.
- Mixing both in one module keeps the stub cost, so the win is per-module and only arrives when the last `kapt(...)` line leaves it.
- The KSP plugin version is pinned to a Kotlin version, like `2.2.20-2.0.4` — a Kotlin bump is now a two-line bump.
- Options move: `kapt { arguments { arg("room.schemaLocation", ...) } }` becomes `ksp { arg(...) }`, and generated code moves to `build/generated/ksp/<variant>/kotlin`, which breaks anything that hardcoded the kapt path.

Measure the module, not the build: `--profile` or a build scan tells you what stubbing costs before you spend a week on the migration.

`buildSrc` is an implicit dependency of every build script in the build, so changing it makes every compiled script class stale and forces a full reconfiguration.

### buildSrc
- Gradle builds `buildSrc` before anything else and puts its output on the classpath of every `build.gradle.kts`. That is why it needs no `includeBuild` line — and why it is felt everywhere.
- Modern Gradle treats it much more like an included build: it participates in the build and configuration caches, and its tests no longer run on every invocation. The classpath relationship is unchanged, though — touch it and every script is out of date.
- It is one project with one classpath, so an Android convention plugin and a two-line CI helper share dependencies and share invalidation.

### An included build
- `pluginManagement { includeBuild("build-logic") }` in `settings.gradle.kts` makes `build-logic` a separate build that publishes plugins by id. It has its own `settings.gradle.kts`, its own dependencies and its own tests, it can be split into several projects, and only scripts that apply a changed plugin are affected.
- Convention plugins live there as a class implementing `Plugin<Project>`, or as a precompiled script named `myapp.android.library.gradle.kts` — the file name becomes the plugin id.
- Declare AGP and the Kotlin plugin `compileOnly` there: `build-logic` compiles against them, but the copy that runs is the one the main build resolves. `implementation` gets you two AGPs on one classpath and a baffling error.

Either way the goal is the same: a feature module's build file should be `plugins { id("myapp.android.feature") }` plus a `dependencies` block, with the SDK levels, the Compose setup and the test wiring stated once. Reach for `build-logic` as soon as the build logic is more than a couple of files — moving it later is mechanical, but the invalidation you pay for in the meantime is not.

It declares no outputs, so Gradle can never call it up to date, and it reaches for the live `Project` at execution time, which is precisely what the configuration cache serialises away.

### Making it incremental
- Every input needs an annotation — `@get:Input` for values, `@get:InputFile` / `@get:InputFiles` / `@get:InputDirectory` for files — and every output needs `@get:OutputFile` or `@get:OutputDirectory`. A task with no declared outputs reruns by definition.
- Use lazy types on `abstract` getters: `Property<T>`, `ListProperty<T>`, `RegularFileProperty`, `DirectoryProperty`. Gradle implements them, and wiring one task's output into another's input through a `Provider` carries the task dependency with it, so you never write `dependsOn`.
- `@CacheableTask` opts into the build cache, and it only pays off with `@PathSensitive(PathSensitivity.RELATIVE)` on file inputs — otherwise absolute paths are part of the cache key and no other checkout, and no CI agent, ever hits.

### Making it configuration-cache safe
The task instance is serialised at the end of configuration and the action runs against that snapshot: at execution time there is no `Project`, no `Gradle`, no resolvable `Configuration`.
- Read what you need at configuration time into properties: `providers.gradleProperty("apiKey")`, `providers.environmentVariable("CI")`, `layout.projectDirectory.file(...)`. Going through `providers` also registers the value as a configuration-cache input, so a changed environment variable invalidates the entry instead of being silently ignored.
- For side effects use injected services instead of `project`: `@get:Inject abstract val fs: FileSystemOperations`, plus `ExecOperations` and `ArchiveOperations`.
- `project.buildDir` inside `@TaskAction` is the classic failure; a `DirectoryProperty` set from `layout.buildDirectory` is the fix.

Rule of thumb: a task that cannot say what it reads and what it writes forces Gradle to assume everything changed — and one whose action needs the build model cannot be replayed from a cache entry at all.

You are missing the configuration cache: the build cache only skips *task* work, and those 45 seconds are the configuration phase, which runs in full on every single invocation until it is cached.

### What each hit skips
- **Configuration cache** serialises the whole task graph — task instances and the fields they hold — keyed by the build's inputs: the scripts, the requested tasks, and every environment variable, system property and file the configuration phase read. A hit skips script evaluation entirely and goes straight to execution.
- **Build cache** hashes each task's declared inputs and stores its outputs under that key. A hit unpacks those outputs instead of running the task, and with a remote node your laptop reuses what CI already compiled.
- They are independent. The build cache pays off on a fresh checkout; the configuration cache pays off on the twentieth run of the same command on your own machine.

### What disqualifies you
- A task action touching `Task.project`, `Gradle` or any other live build-model object. Capture what the action needs into `Property`/`Provider` fields at configuration time instead.
- Reading environment variables, system properties or files outside the provider API. `providers.environmentVariable(...)` and `providers.exec {}` are tracked as inputs; a bare `System.getenv` in a task action is invisible to both caches.
- For the build cache: a task with no declared outputs, with undeclared inputs, or with absolute paths baked into its inputs — that last one is why CI's entries never match a laptop's.
- `@CacheableTask` is opt-in. Without it a perfectly correct task is simply never cached.

Prove it rather than assume it: run the build twice and read the `--scan` performance tab, which splits wall time into configuration and execution and labels every task `FROM-CACHE`, `UP-TO-DATE` or `EXECUTED`. `build/reports/configuration-cache/**/configuration-cache-report.html` lists each problem with the code that caused it, and `--configuration-cache-problems=fail` stops new ones creeping back.

Almost none of it is compiling your line: an incremental build is configuration time, plus everything your change invalidated downstream, plus a serial `:app` tail that no amount of parallelism touches.

### Measure before you refactor
- `--scan` gives you a timeline of what ran when and on which worker; `--profile` is the offline version. Read the **critical path**, not the sum of task times — sixty tasks on eight workers cost you the longest chain.
- If configuration alone is 40 seconds on every invocation, the configuration cache is your first win and no module surgery is needed yet.
- Reproduce a realistic change (touch one Kotlin file in a leaf module) rather than timing a clean build; they have completely different profiles.

### Where the minutes usually are
- **The graph is a chain, not a fan.** If `:feature:checkout` depends on `:feature:cart`, Gradle cannot start them together. Features that depend only on small `:core` modules compile in parallel; features that depend on each other serialise.
- **ABI changes.** Kotlin's compile avoidance skips a consumer when the producer's public signatures are unchanged, so an internal-only edit is cheap and a public one is not. `api` propagates that recompilation one level further than `implementation` does.
- **Annotation processing.** kapt generates Java stubs for the whole module before processing; KSP is the replacement. Aggregating processors — Hilt's component assembly at `:app` — mean every module's change lands back in the app.
- **The `:app` tail.** Manifest merging, resource merging, dexing and packaging are serial and always last. Never enable `minifyEnabled` on debug, and keep `android.nonTransitiveRClass=true` so an R class change does not touch everything.

Order of attack: configuration cache, then build cache local and remote, then `org.gradle.parallel=true` and enough heap in `org.gradle.jvmargs` (a GC-thrashing daemon reads exactly like a slow compiler), then flatten the module graph. Module surgery is the expensive lever, so it goes last.

It separates what a feature compiles against from what actually changes: features see only the tiny `api` module's signatures, so churn inside `impl` never reaches their compile classpath, and `:app` is the single place the two meet.

### What the graph gains
- `:feature:*` depends on `:core:cart:api` and nothing else; `:app` depends on both and hosts the `@Binds` that connects them. The compiler now enforces a layering that code review would otherwise have to police.
- An api module is interfaces, models and error types. Its ABI moves rarely, so compile avoidance keeps every feature out of the rebuild while impl-only code churns daily.
- A second implementation costs nothing: a fake for tests, an offline variant, a stub for a feature flag. Consumers do not change at all.
- The price is configuration time and task count. Forty modules become eighty, each with its own configuration, its own Kotlin compile task and its own build directory.

### When it is ceremony
- One implementation, a stable interface, no test double. Compile avoidance already skips consumers for non-ABI changes, so the split buys almost nothing that `internal` inside one module would not.
- Modules that are only data — models, `Result` types, constants. There is no implementation to hide.
- An api module that has to expose Retrofit, Room or Compose types in its signatures. It is no longer a thin ABI, it drags the same dependencies onto every consumer, and the split has become a rename.

Rule of thumb: split when somebody other than `:app` needs to swap the implementation, or when a hot impl has many consumers. Otherwise ship one module and mark the internals `internal` — in Kotlin that already means "invisible outside this Gradle module".

A version conflict and a duplicate class are different failures: Gradle resolves a conflict by picking the highest requested version of one module, but two *different* modules that happen to contain the same class are not a conflict it can see, so the collision only surfaces when D8 merges the classpath.

### Finding out who asked for what
- `./gradlew :app:dependencyInsight --configuration releaseRuntimeClasspath --dependency kotlin-stdlib` prints every requester and the reason a version won: "by conflict resolution", "by constraint", "forced".
- `./gradlew :app:dependencies --configuration releaseRuntimeClasspath` dumps the whole tree. Pick the runtime classpath for a packaging or dexing failure and the compile classpath for a compile error — they resolve independently and can differ.
- Gradle's default is highest-wins across the entire graph, not Maven's nearest-first. A transitive `1.4` plus your `1.9` gives everyone 1.9, which is usually right and occasionally the reason something broke.

### The fixes, best first
- **Module replacement** is the honest answer to a duplicate class: tell Gradle the two coordinates are the same artifact. Here, `kotlin-stdlib-jdk7`/`jdk8` were folded into `kotlin-stdlib` in Kotlin 1.8, so an old library still asking for them collides with your current stdlib.
- **A constraint with `strictly`** pins a version and records why, so `dependencyInsight` still shows the requesters. `resolutionStrategy.force` is the blunt version and hides them.
- **`exclude`** on the dependency that drags in the copy, when you cannot bump it.
- **A `platform()` BOM** keeps a family aligned so there is no conflict to resolve in the first place, and `failOnVersionConflict()` turns a silent upgrade into a build failure.

`packaging { resources { excludes += ... } }` is not a fix here. It deduplicates META-INF *resources*; duplicate *classes* are a dexing problem and excluding a resource just hides the symptom.

A build that resolves from the network is only as reproducible as the repositories behind it; locking, checksum verification and a blocking dependency report are what turn "a transitive dependency moved" into a failed CI job instead of a mystery.

### Pinning what actually resolves
- **Dependency locking** — `dependencyLocking { lockAllConfigurations() }` plus `./gradlew dependencies --write-locks` writes a `gradle.lockfile` holding the exact resolved graph, transitives included. After that, a changed transitive version fails the build until someone regenerates the lockfile in a reviewable diff.
- **Verification metadata** — `./gradlew --write-verification-metadata sha256 help` produces `gradle/verification-metadata.xml`, and Gradle then rejects any artifact whose checksum has changed. That is the supply-chain half of the same problem.
- **Ban moving targets** — `resolutionStrategy.failOnNonReproducibleResolution()` covers both dynamic versions (`1.+`, `latest.release`) and changing ones (`-SNAPSHOT`). A version catalog helps only if nobody writes a range into it; `coil = "2.+"` in `libs.versions.toml` is still a time bomb.

### Keeping the graph honest
- The dependency-analysis plugin's `buildHealth` task reports dependencies you declare but never use, `api` that should be `implementation`, and transitive types you use without declaring — the three things that quietly widen every consumer's classpath and slow the build.
- A module-graph assertion fails a pull request that adds a forbidden edge: a `:core` module reaching into a `:feature`, or a graph deeper than the height you agreed on.
- Both run in CI as blocking checks, not as a nightly report. A rule nobody fails on is a rule that decays within a month.

The rule of thumb behind all of it: a dependency change should arrive as a pull request with a lockfile diff — from Renovate or Dependabot — never as a side effect of running the same build on a different day.

Three things the default setup will not give you: a variant-aware component so consumers resolve the right artifact, consumer ProGuard rules packaged inside the AAR, and a committed ABI dump so you learn you broke someone before they do.

### Publishing the variant
- AGP creates no publishable component until you ask for one: `android { publishing { singleVariant("release") { withSourcesJar(); withJavadocJar() } } }`, then a `MavenPublication` with `from(components["release"])`. The component only exists after AGP has evaluated, which is why the `from(...)` usually sits in `afterEvaluate`.
- Gradle Module Metadata — the `.module` file published beside the POM — carries the api/runtime split, the target JVM and, with `multipleVariants`, one entry per flavor. A consumer resolving through a plain POM loses all of that, which is where "it works in one project and not the other" begins.
- Publish `debug` only if somebody genuinely needs it. Every extra variant is another artifact you have to keep alive forever.

### What travels inside the AAR
- `consumerProguardFiles("consumer-rules.pro")` bakes your keep rules into the AAR as `proguard.txt`, and the consumer's R8 run applies them automatically. Without it, every consumer discovers your reflection at runtime, in release, on a user's phone.
- Ship only rules your own code needs. A `-dontobfuscate` or a broad `-keep class **` inside an AAR silently ruins the size of every app that depends on you.
- Your manifest merges into theirs — permissions, `<provider>` entries, `<queries>` — so treat it as public API too.

### Not breaking them
- `binary-compatibility-validator` commits a `.api` file: `apiDump` regenerates it and `apiCheck` fails the pull request that changed a public signature without anyone noticing. Kotlin 2.2 began folding the same check into the Kotlin plugin behind an experimental `abiValidation` block.
- Mark everything you did not mean to expose `internal`. A public `data class` pins `copy()` and every `componentN()`, and adding a parameter with a default value is source-compatible but binary-incompatible — old consumers call a signature that no longer exists.

It inverted the dependency: a dynamic feature depends on the base `:app`, not the other way round, so the base can never import a feature type and everything crossing that boundary goes through an interface the base owns, an implicit intent, or reflection.

### What changes in the build
- `:app` declares `android { dynamicFeatures += setOf(":feature:scan") }`; the feature applies `com.android.dynamic-feature` and declares `implementation(project(":app"))`.
- A dynamic feature has no build types or flavors of its own — it inherits the base's variants, signing, versioning and `minifyEnabled`. R8 runs once across base and features together, so a keep rule in the base covers both.
- Delivery mode lives in the feature's manifest: `<dist:module>` with `<dist:on-demand/>`, or `<dist:install-time>` with `<dist:conditions>` for min-SDK, a device feature or a country list.
- The artifact is an app bundle. `assembleRelease` produces an APK with no delivery at all; you need `bundleRelease`, and `bundletool` to install one locally.

### What changes at runtime
- `SplitInstallManager` (from `com.google.android.play:feature-delivery`, since the monolithic Play Core artifact was split up) requests the module. It is a UI flow, not a function call: you must handle `DOWNLOADING`, `REQUIRES_USER_CONFIRMATION`, `INSTALLED` and failure.
- Call `SplitCompat.installActivity(this)`, or extend `SplitCompatApplication`, or the newly installed module's resources stay invisible until the process restarts.
- The entry point is resolved by name — `Class.forName("com.example.scan.ScanActivity")` or an implicit intent — because the base has no compile-time handle on it.

The debug trap: Android Studio installs every split with `adb install-multiple`, so on-demand modules are already present and your request "succeeds" instantly. You never exercise the download, the confirmation dialog or the failure path. Test those with `FakeSplitInstallManagerFactory` from the library's testing package, and on a real device through an internal test track — the local build proves nothing.

Pin every input the build takes from the machine — the JDK, the Gradle distribution, the plugin versions and the daemon's memory — so the only thing that differs between a laptop and an agent is the source tree.

### The JDK is two different things
- The JDK that *runs* Gradle (whatever `JAVA_HOME` points at) and the JDK that *compiles* your code are separate. Fix the second with a toolchain: `java { toolchain { languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(17) } }` and `kotlin { jvmToolchain(17) }`. Gradle then provisions that exact JDK or fails loudly, instead of compiling with whatever it found.
- A mismatched `jvmTarget` between Java and Kotlin compilation is exactly this bug, and a toolchain sets both from one place. Add the foojay resolver in `settings.gradle.kts` so a machine without that JDK can download it; on CI, pre-install it and set `org.gradle.java.installations.auto-download=false` so a network hiccup is not a build failure.

### Everything else that drifts
- Commit the wrapper and put `distributionSha256Sum` in `gradle-wrapper.properties`. Run `./gradlew`, never a locally installed `gradle`.
- Put AGP, Kotlin and KSP in the version catalog so they move together — a KSP version is bound to one exact Kotlin version, and since Kotlin 2.0 the Compose compiler ships with Kotlin itself.
- Keep `org.gradle.jvmargs` in the committed `gradle.properties`, not in a personal one. A different heap means a different daemon, and an OOM on CI reads like a compiler bug.
- macOS is case-insensitive and Linux is not, so `import com.example.Foo` against a file that declares `foo` compiles on a laptop and fails on the agent.

### Why the remote cache misses
- The toolchain version is part of a compile task's cache key, so a JDK 17.0.9 laptop and a JDK 17.0.13 agent share nothing.
- Absolute paths in task inputs, a `BuildConfig` build timestamp, or a git-describe string recomputed per build all poison the key. Declare inputs `@PathSensitive(PathSensitivity.RELATIVE)` and make generated files deterministic.
- Two build scans — one local, one from CI — compared side by side name the exact input that differed. That is what the comparison view exists for.
